title: Vicon Acquires Facial Capture Firm Captive Devices (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Vicon has acquired Captive Devices Ltd, a Manchester, U.K.-based maker of head-mounted camera systems for markerless facial performance capture.
body:
Vicon has acquired Captive Devices Ltd, a Manchester, U.K.-based maker of head-mounted camera systems for markerless facial performance capture. 

	Vicon is the motion capture arm of Oxford Metrics. The founding team at Captive Devices has joined Vicon effective immediately.

	Ninja Theory, Nant Studios, Animatrik and Deep Silver Dambuster Studios are among the studios that already rely on Captive Devices’ hardware and software to capture facial performance for visual effects, games and virtual production. Folding that technology into Vicon’s existing body-tracking systems gives the company an in-house offering that spans both facial and body capture, something it says no other vendor in the space currently provides.
	

	Vicon’s marker-based optical motion capture, the core of its business for more than 40 years, remains unchanged. The company frames the acquisition as an addition rather than a replacement, allowing customers to layer markerless facial capture onto the systems they already run.


	“This acquisition is a natural fit for Vicon and Captive Devices, culturally and technologically,” said Imogen O’Connor, chief executive of Oxford Metrics, Vicon’s parent company. “Vicon can now offer customers a more integrated, end-to-end body and face capture workflow that enables them to capture, analyze and animate human performance with even greater efficiency than before.”

	David “Ed” Edwards, product lead for entertainment and hardware at Vicon, pointed to a long-standing split in how studios have sourced facial and body capture. “This pairing closes a real gap for studios in film, games and virtual production,” Edwards said. “Body and facial performance capture have always come from separate vendors with separate pipelines. Now it’s one system, one team and one support line.”
	

	The CoreHMC system built by Captive Devices plugs directly into Epic Games’ Unreal Engine, letting performers and crews capture, review and tweak facial performance in real time on set. That integration means studios already working in Unreal Engine pipelines can begin using the technology without a transition period.

	Fred Isaac, co-founder of Captive Devices, said the deal extends the reach of that hardware. “Joining Vicon gives us the manufacturing scale, sales distribution and global support network to put CoreHMC in front of far more studios than we could reach alone,” Isaac said. “The technology, the team and the way we serve customers remains the same. Now we’re joining a team who’s spent decades building trust with exactly the studios we want to reach.”

	O’Connor described the acquisition as part of a broader investment strategy at Vicon. “These are exactly the kind of targeted investments we want to make in Vicon – adding differentiated technology and specialist expertise in areas that build seamlessly onto our existing strengths,” she said.

	Vicon was founded in 1984 and builds motion capture systems for use in life sciences, entertainment, location-based virtual reality and engineering. Its client list spans Dreamworks, Byte Dance, Electronic Arts, Epic Games, Industrial Light and Magic, Lux Machina, Pearl Abyss, Sony, Ubisoft and Warner Bros. Oxford Metrics, its parent company, serves thousands of customers across more than 70 countries.

title: Isabelle Huppert, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Kore-Eda Hirokazu, Fan Bingbing, Michelle Yeoh on Guest List as Busan Unveils Galas, Asian Cinema Competition
description: The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled a guest lineup headlined by Isabelle Huppert, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Kore-eda Hirokazu, F
body:
The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled a guest lineup headlined by Isabelle Huppert, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Kore-eda Hirokazu, Fan Bingbing and Michelle Yeoh.

	Huppert brings her latest film, “All About Corinne,” to Busan audiences. Gyllenhaal makes her first visit to Korea with “Flesh Impact,” a project created to mark the centenary of Marilyn Monroe’s birth. Fan Bingbing joins fellow Chinese stars Shu Qi and Zhou Xun in Busan, while also curating a Carte Blanche selection of Park Chan-wook’s “The Handmaiden.” Yeoh, the first Asian performer to win the Academy Award for best actress, returns to the festival after 15 years to receive the Asian Filmmaker of the Year award and appears in the gala presentation title “It’s My Time.”
	

	The broader guest roster runs deep. Hong Kong’s Ann Hui will accept the Camellia Award, and Indonesian icon Christine Hakim will also attend. Iranian director Majid Majidi, known for “Children of Heaven,” makes his first trip to Korea with competition entry “Midday Meal.” Animator Rintaro returns to discuss his work on “Metropolis,” and Filipino director Lav Diaz comes back to Korea after a decade away. Japan’s Kore-eda Hirokazu arrives with “Look Back,” Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang returns for a second straight year with a new entry in his “Walker” series, and French filmmaker Bertrand Mandico brings “Roma Elastica,” starring Marion Cotillard. Korean auteurs Lee Chang-dong, Na Hong-Jin and Kim Jeewoon round out the lineup, the latter appearing as one of this year’s three Carte Blanche curators.


	Japan sends a large delegation of stars led by Nagasawa Masami, including Emoto Tasuku, Ishibashi Shizuka, Kuroki Haru, Yokohama Ryusei, Yamazaki Kento, Matsushita Kouhei, Sawajiri Erika, Maruyama Ryuhei and Nagayama Eita. A younger group of international names is also set to attend, among them Yeh Shuhua, Michelle Mao, Jin Ha and Thai star Davika Hoorne.
	

	BIFF’s gala presentation section will screen five films with their directors and casts in attendance. Kore-eda’s “Look Back” adapts Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga for the screen. “All About Corinne,” from director Marc Fitoussi, marks his fourth collaboration with Huppert. Judith Godrèche’s “A Girl’s Story” revisits Nobel laureate Annie Ernaux’s most intimate memories to follow a young woman’s coming of age. “It’s My Time,” from director Bai Xue, casts Yeoh as a 70-year-old woman taking on an unexpected challenge. July Jung’s “Dora,” which premiered at Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight, closes out the section.

	BIFF’s competition section, its main Asian cinema showcase, features 14 films from Korea, Japan, China, Taiwan, Iran, Uzbekistan and Indonesia, four of them directorial debuts and four from women filmmakers. Majidi’s “Midday Meal” anchors an international lineup that includes Kato Takuya’s “The Day After Sunday,” Chen Jiwen’s “Descendants,” Gu You’s “The First Taste of Loneliness,” Hirose Nanako’s “Between Two Lovers,” Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” Okita Shuichi’s “Satoko Always,” Yosep Anggi Noen’s “The Sea Speaks His Name,” Kim Jung-hoon’s “Shaving” and Lee Yun Chan’s “To Be Ordinary.” The four debut features come from Lim Hayeon, Botir Abdurakhmanov, Youm Kyubock and Tanaka Miki. The section serves as the entry point for BIFF’s New Currents Award, given to a standout directorial debut.

	Alongside competition, the festival’s Window on Asian Cinema section adds 28 further titles from established and emerging filmmakers working across Asia and its diaspora, many of them multi-country co-productions. The lineup includes Wayne Wang’s “Diary of a Mad Old Man,” Kamila Andini’s “Four Seasons in Java,” Rima Das’ “Not a Hero” and Fujii Michihito’s “You, Like a Star,” alongside a broad spread of titles spanning India, Japan, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam, Kazakhstan, Iran and beyond.

	BIFF’s Icons section, its sidebar for works by established masters of world cinema, presents 35 films this year. The lineup brings together Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s “All of a Sudden,” Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas,” Werner Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard,” Lukas Dhont’s “Coward,” Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” David Lowery’s “Mother Mary,” starring Anne Hathaway, and Brad Bird’s animated “Ray Gunn,” featuring the voices of Sam Rockwell, Scarlett Johansson and Tom Waits. It also includes Korean auteurs Hong Sangsoo and Lee Chang-dong, Taiwan’s Tsai Ming-liang, and Kogonada’s U.S.-Hong Kong co-production “Zi,” which will have its international premiere in Busan.
	

	The festival’s guest and program announcements follow a run of earlier reveals for this year’s edition, including the “The Table: Day and Night” opening film, the Vision-Korea and Vision-Asia lineups, the Korean Cinema Today and On Screen selections, the Carte Blanche curators, a tribute program for the late Ahn Sung-ki, and market-side news from the Asian Contents & Film Market, including Thailand’s debut as Country of Honor, the InnoAsia technology program and new additions to the Asian Project Market and Busan Story Market.

	The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15 at the Busan Cinema Center and venues throughout Busan, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13.

	COMPETITION SELECTION 

	“Beach Fictions” – Lim Hayeon – Korea – World Premiere“Between Two Lovers” – Hirose Nanako – Japan – World Premiere“The Day After Sunday” – Kato Takuya – Japan / France – World Premiere“Descendants” – Chen Jiwen – China – World Premiere“The First Taste of Loneliness” – Gu You – China – World Premiere“Hilol” – Botir Abdurakhmanov – Uzbekistan – World Premiere“Ibuku” – Eddie Cahyono – Indonesia / Japan – World Premiere“Long Long Night” – Youm Kyubock – Korea“Midday Meal” – Majid Majidi – Iran – World Premiere“Satoko Always” – Okita Shuichi – Japan – International Premiere“The Sea Speaks His Name” – Yosep Anggi Noen – Indonesia – World Premiere“Shaving” – Kim Jung-hoon – Korea – World Premiere“Silver Express” – Tanaka Miki – Japan – World Premiere“To Be Ordinary” – Lee Yun Chan – Taiwan – World Premiere

title: Mexico’s Martfilms Boards ‘Looking for Sam,’ Mariana Rondón’s Follow-Up to ‘Bad Hair’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Mexico’s Martfilms has boarded “Looking for Sam,” Mariana Rondón’s follow-up to her acclaimed coming -of-age drama “Bad Hair” (“Pelo malo”).

	A doc
body:
Mexico’s Martfilms has boarded “Looking for Sam,” Mariana Rondón’s follow-up to her acclaimed coming -of-age drama “Bad Hair” (“Pelo malo”).

	A docu-fiction hybrid bound for San Sebastian’s Europe-Latin America Co-Production Forum, the drama follows two lead actors from Mariana Rondón’s 2013 San Sebastian Golden Shell winner “Bad Hair” (“Pelo Malo”): Sam Lange who played the child Junior and the actress who played his mother, Samantha Castillo. Both of them were forced to leave Venezuela.
	

	“’Looking for Sam’ wanders between fiction and documentary, where memory and identity blur and transform one another. It forces us to ask ourselves who we are when we leave behind who we once were,” Rondón told Variety.


	“The film is about crossing borders: geographical, temporal, bodily and borders of identity. We are not simply looking for Sam. We are searching for the place where the person we once were ends and the person we are begins,” said her producing partner Marite Ugás of Sudaca Films, who added that they found Lange walking the fashion runways of Paris while Castillo emigrated to Mexico.

	For Martfilm’s Martha Orozco, the partnership was a long time coming. “I’ve been following the career of this talented duo and our filmographies have often brought us together on our cinematic journeys. We’ve wanted to collaborate for a long time, and this project allows us to experiment creatively.”

	“’Bad Hair,” beyond being a successful film, was a bold film for its time – one that dared to address racism, homophobia and polarization, leaving its mark on Latin American cinema. On a personal level, this inspired me to believe in resilient cinema, and through MartFilms, it’s a pleasure to be part of this new phase and share new experiences,” Orozco said, adding: “’Looking for Sam’ will be a nostalgic reunion – the country has changed, the protagonists have grown up and Mariana and Marité’s filmmaking has matured – so we expect nothing but good things from this journey.”
	

	Martfilms has participated in past industry forums at San Sebastián, winning the pix-in-post WIP award with the Argentine-Mexican co-production “Pornomelancholia” by Manuel Abramovich and snagging the Forum prize with Laura Baumeister’s feature debut “Daughter of Rage” (Nicaragua/Mexico).

	According to Ugás, Sudaca Films was invited to the “Écritures” Residency at the Cité internationale des arts in Paris for 2026–2027, starting this December.

	The six-month residency will allow them to continue working on the screenplay, but also to spend time with Lange, who currently lives in Paris.

	“That’s why it is particularly important for us to meet a French partner at the Europe-Latin America Co-production Forum,” said Ugás who is co-writing the screenplay with Rondón.

	Founded by Rondón and Ugás, Sudaca Films turned 30 this year and is also known for such acclaimed pics as Tribeca 2021 title “Contactado” and “Zafari,” which won the French Film Critics Award in 2024.

	Martfilms, which is dedicated to the creation and distribution of films committed to diversity, inclusion and social transformation has produced such films as “Beyond My Grandfather Allende” (“Allende mi abuelo Allende”) a Chile-Mexico co-production that won the best documentary L’Œil d’Or at the 2015 Cannes Film Festival and “Niñxs” (Mexico), among others.

	The 74th San Sebastian Film Festival runs over Sept. 18-26.



	

					(l-r) Mariana Rondón and Marité Ugas of Sudaca Films Credit: Lima Film Festival

title: Sandra Bullock Recalls First ‘Practical Magic’ Bombing After Thinking ‘People Are Going to Love It’: ‘And Then It Got Quiet’
description: The Owen sisters may be back in “Practical Magic 2” 28 years after Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock first played the sibling witches, but that doesn
body:
The Owen sisters may be back in “Practical Magic 2” 28 years after Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock first played the sibling witches, but that doesn’t mean the first movie’s outing doesn’t still sting a little.

	The original “Practical Magic” was a critical and box office failure before earning cult classic status over the last almost three decades.

	“We thought, ‘This is going to be such an amazing film. People are going to love it,’” Bullock recalled. “And then it got quiet. It got quiet. [They] were like, ‘How many women in a film do you need? How many tones do you need? What kind of film is this?’”
	

	“And here’s the thing that I really wanna bring up and I bring it up ad nauseam: Griffin Dunne created this world with us,” Bullock said, referring to the first film’s director.


	Kidman added, “And he loved us and he let us shine.”

	Bullock continued, “It’s because of him, this film exists, and he never got to smell the flowers when we made it. So tonight we’re honoring him.”


	Why did they decide to make the sequel now?

	“It just happened,” Kidman said. It was more like serendipity, and it came, and we were ready, and everything fell into place. It’s like in life — you try to force things; it doesn’t work. You have to wait, be patient, and we both kind of open to it.”

	“Practical Magic 2” is based on Alice Hoffman’s novel “The Book of Magic.” Directed by Susanne Bier, the film sees the return of original stars Kidman, Bullock, Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest. Newcomers include Joey King, Maisie Williams, Lee Pace, Xolo Maridueña and Solly McLeod.
	

Joey King calls her relationship with Nicole Kidman a “pinch me moment” at the #PracticalMagic2 premiere“When you have someone who has been through so much, who is open and loving with their knowledge, I couldn’t be more grateful. I feel so lucky to be able to go to her.” pic.twitter.com/s18jILGzDy— Variety (@Variety) September 1, 2026


	This is the second time King worked with Kidman following the 2024 rom-com “Family Affair” with Zac Efron. “When you have someone who has been through so much, who is open and loving with their knowledge, I couldn’t be more grateful,” King told me about her relationship with Kidman. “I feel so lucky to be able to go to her.”

title: The Rise of ‘Love Island USA’: From Death Threats Against Contestants to Agency Battles for the Biggest Stars
description: When Liv Walker first heard from the “Love Island USA” casting team, she thought it might be a scam. After all, she had never even seen the show.
body:
When Liv Walker first heard from the “Love Island USA” casting team, she thought it might be a scam. After all, she had never even seen the show.

	Originally scouted for Season 5 of the reality dating show, Walker turned down the initial offer. But when the casting team reached out again for the sixth season a year later in 2024, she decided to give the show a shot.

	That decision changed her life. 

	Season 6 went on to transform the U.S. installment of “Love Island,” distinguishing itself from the U.K. version that had popularized the idea of dropping a group of young, ready-to-mingle strangers together into a private villa cut off from the outside world.

	“Love Island USA” originally aired on CBS when the show launched in 2019, with comedian Arielle Vandenberg hosting. The series switched to Peacock for its fourth season, replacing Vandenberg with Sarah Hyland — before Ariana Madix officially took over as host in Season 6. Following her dramatic break-up with Tom Sandoval, the “Vanderpump Rules” star brought the Bravo audience over to Peacock, and the dynamic cast kept them watching. 

	“When I first got kicked off the show, I remember one of the talent managers was like, ‘Hi! Just a head’s up, the show did better than ‘Bridgerton,’” Walker tells Variety. “I was like, ‘What do you mean, better?’”


	Season 6 of “Love Island USA,” which is produced by ITV America and airs on Peacock every summer, saw its viewership double compared to that of previous seasons, according to NBCUniversal. Those numbers have only continued to grow in the two years since. This past summer, Season 8 drew 19 billion minutes watched, translating to 7.9 million views, according to data from Peacock.

	The newly Bravo-fied “Aftersun” spinoff, now co-hosted by “Summer House” star Ciara Miller, saw a 135% increase in viewership from last season. And with other spinoff series such as “Beyond the Villa” and “Love Island Games,” many Islanders continue their journey far beyond their original seasons.


	For Walker, Season 6 was the beginning of what she calls “the catapult.” For the franchise, it was the beginning of a transformation from a reality dating series into something much larger — one that would transform its contestants into global celebrities and content creators in the process.


	“I don’t think we’ve seen anything quite like this,” says UTA unscripted TV agent Jamie Youngentob. “The closest thing would probably be Bravo, but those shows can take multiple seasons for somebody to really break through and stick.”



	

					Season 6: Daniela Noelle Ortiz-Rivera, Leah Kateb, Kaylor Martin 
									Courtesy of Ben Symons/Peacock
	



	The Season That Changed Everything
	

	Season 6 had taken the world by storm, but its success wasn’t the result of contestants entering the villa with dreams of becoming influencers. In fact, several of the season’s Islanders say the opposite was true: They had no idea anyone would be watching at the scale they ultimately were.

	Kaylor Martin, who appeared alongside Walker in Season 6, was a senior in college when she applied. She was working three jobs, had about 4,000 Instagram followers and rarely posted on social media. 

	“I don’t think any of us had expectations on our lives being changed,” Martin tells Variety, noting that she and her fellow Islanders had plans to return to work or school after the show. 
	

	That naivete, she believes, is part of what made Season 6 resonate. The cast wasn’t performing for an audience they knew was watching.

	“If I wasn’t on Season 6, and I was asked to go on Season 7 or 8, I don’t know if I would have cried that much or acted so organically because we truly had no idea everyone was watching,” Martin says.

	The result was a group of contestants whose lives changed almost overnight. Martin went from being a college student to, two years after leaving the villa, working as a full-time content creator and host of the podcast, “Kaylor’s Crash Out Podcast.” 

	Nobody expected Season 6’s spike in popularity, including creatives and talent agencies. When Martin left the villa, she didn’t prioritize brand deals or posting consistently because she didn’t realize social media could become a career. 

	She says “Love Island” now helps its contestants navigate the transition, connecting Islanders with agencies and publicists after they leave the show — something Season 6 didn’t offer. After having to navigate that process largely on her own, Martin is now eager to help Islanders from recent seasons with their post-villa journey. Most recently, she connected with Season 8 contestant Kenzie Annis and gave her advice on growing her platform. 

	Now, leading talent agencies view “Love Island” as a viable pipeline for creators looking to build long-term careers. It has become an increasingly competitive space to scoop up talent, says UTA partner and agent Mahzad Babayan, with the agency signing Season 8 winner Bryce Alakai just over a week after the finale aired. Gersh, meanwhile, reps Emmy-nominated host Madix and Season 8 contestant Annis.

	But for agents working in the digital creator space, it’s not about securing the buzziest “Love Island” Islanders with the biggest brand deals — it’s about finding the right talent who are looking for longevity over a viral moment, far past the one-year exclusivity deal that limits what opportunities “Love Island” contestants can take. That usually means keeping them in the NBCUniversal family.

	“The talent know, now more than ever, what they’re getting into,” says Gersh’s head of digital Jade Sherman. “‘Love Island’ is an incredible brand, and they try really hard to protect their IP. They’ve put things in place to do that, and it’s on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are.”

	For UTA, signing Alakai was attractive because he already had a “real” career in music before going on the show, and even appeared in a Tubi film. 

	“He’s been working incredibly hard at pursuing and building a DJ career,” Youngentob says. “That was exciting for us, alongside our music colleagues.”
	

	The Islanders who followed in Seasons 7 and 8 entered a franchise that was already a proven launching pad to worldwide fame and opportunity.

	Amaya, who won Season 7, was working as a registered nurse when a casting producer reached out to her. Like Walker, she had never watched a full season of “Love Island,” and her exposure to the show primarily stemming from viral clips on social media. 

	Unlike the Season 6 cast, though, Amaya entered the villa knowing what the previous season had become. But the show’s newfound fame didn’t sway her decision to apply.

	“I feel like life is all about taking risk,” she tells Variety about deciding to join the show. “You just have to trust your intuition, and it was the best thing I did.”

	After becoming a fan favorite of Season 7 and being crowned its winner, Amaya was determined to pursue other opportunities beyond reality television. She’s now working on music, exploring her passion for poetry and taking acting classes, all opportunities that launched from her time on the show. 

	“Thank God I decided to take the chance and to take the risk and to not let self-doubt hold me back,” she says. “That’s just the message that I’m trying to give overall — ‘Why not?’” 

	Starring alongside Amaya in Season 7 was Iris Kendall, who was originally scouted for Season 6 but declined. When she decided to accept the offer for the seventh season, the success of the previous season made her anxious about stepping into the public eye. 

	“Honestly, in a perfect world, if it wasn’t filmed and I did the social experiment, that would be freaking awesome,” Kendall tells Variety, laughing. “But it definitely made me nervous to be in the public eye and have people critique every single thing that I could possibly do, especially when the cameras are on you 24/7.”
	

	By the time Kendall left the villa, the scale of the franchise had grown even larger. At the Season 7 finale, the cast was told the season had performed seven times better than the previous one.

	And the opportunities followed. Kendall signed with WME and turned what she expected might be a handful of brand deals into a full-time career.

	“I just thought I’m going to get maybe some deals here and there, but I didn’t think that I was going to be doing anything that I’m doing now or having this as a full time career,” she says about her success after the show. “I’m just so thankful that I put myself out there to the public.”



	

									Courtesy of Peacock
	



	Fame Has a Price

	But underneath the brand deals and business ventures lies an increasingly attached fanbase analyzing the Islanders’ every move. After getting her phone back and seeing the world’s reaction to Season 7, Kendall says she quickly learned that fans could develop strong opinions about Islanders based solely on what they’ve seen on television and social media. 

	“We have parasocial people commenting on our lives,” Kendall says. “They don’t really know us. They don’t know what we text about. They don’t know what we talk about.”

	While the Islanders are in the villa, they’re completely oblivious to the fact that an entirely new universe forms on social media among those tuned into the show. Viewers take it upon themselves to determine who the token heroes and villains of the season are, often fighting over just how well a contestant should be liked. 

	In Season 7, fans notably targeted contestant Huda Mustafa, turning her vulnerable moments into widespread memes (yes, we’re talking about her “dream date”). In Season 6, fans honed in on Andrea Carmona, quickly labeling her as an antagonist.

	“I was not expecting that. I had to get off of social media for two weeks,” Carmona tells Variety. “My TikTok for you page was just people saying very nasty things about me, and this whole narrative that I knew in my heart wasn’t me. But at the end of the day, people are going to perceive you however they want.”

	The feeling that viewers personally know the people they’re watching on screen could stem in part from the fact that the show is on six days a week each summer, which gives audiences hours upon hours of consistent access to the Islanders’ lives.
	

	“Younger fans are drawn to it as appointment-viewing television, because a lot of what is transpiring on screen are relationship dynamics that they might identify with themselves, so there is a lot of projection onto the cast of characters. And that creates an entirely new show,” says Brandy Monk-Payton, assistant professor at Fordham University. “It’s almost as if there is the show that exists on Peacock, and the show that exists on TikTok.” 

	Danielle J. Lindemann, the author of “What Reality TV Says About Us,” adds, “There’s this whole other discourse happening online that you almost have to follow in order to watch and understand the show. You kind of have to do them both in tandem.”

	Additionally, viewers engage with “Love Island” on a much higher, more intense level than other reality dating shows because they’re able to directly vote on which couples they want to stay together and, ultimately, which couple takes home $100,000 on finale night.

	“Who you enjoy, who you want to win, becomes a projection of your identity and so you have all of these conflicts online that are just proxy wars,” Bonk-Payton adds.

	Carmona says that, even two years after her season, she still gets hate messages from those still parasocially attached to Season 6. 

	“I generally say from my season, I’m happy that I was the one that got all this hate because truthfully, I don’t think anyone on that season could have handled the amount that I got and still be here today. That’s how bad it was.”

	Daniella Bondar, an admin of a “Love Island” Facebook group with more than 300,000 members, says that people get reported every day for hateful comments, although she notes that the group remains mostly positive and cordial. Discourse in the group continues long after the show airs, with members keeping up with the contestants from past seasons via social media and clamoring for details about their lives.

	“When I watched the show, I didn’t know what the problems with Zach were, but then I go to the group and I see the big discussion is that everybody thinks he’s here just to be on social media, just to be famous, they didn’t like him,” Bondar says. “They’re taking all the things they see on TikTok and Instagram and then bringing it back into the group to see how everybody else feels.”

	False narratives and misconceptions are common in “Love Island,” largely stemming from the fact that Peacock creatives are tasked with condensing 24 hours of footage into one-hour episodes. That sometimes means key elements of a contestant’s personalities, their relationship dynamics and their friendships don’t make it into the final cut. 
	

	“What matters the most to me is how the people in my life view me, how I treat other people, and if I’m doing a good job at that,” Kendall says about receiving negativity from viewers with false perceptions of her. “That’s what’s important to me, not what random people say or what random people think.”

	To help control the negative comments online and bullying online, Peacock released a statement ahead of Season 8 prior to the first episode airing, reminding fans to “keep it kind” and “keep it positive.” A similar statement was released in Season 7, reminding fans that the Islanders are “real people.” 



	

					Season 7
									Courtesy of Jocelyn Prescod/Peacock
	



	Building Community

	With the Season 8 reunion dropping on Aug. 31, the Islanders — who have strategically been quieter on social media than contestants from past seasons, and have done limited press in the lead-up to the reunion — are ready to move into the next phase of their lives outside the “Love Island” bubble.

	Unlike Walker, who might as well have appeared on an entirely different show than what the Season 5 Islanders experienced, contestants who get off the show now know they have a community of past “Love Island” Islanders to connect with. 

	That’s an especially important point for Carmona, who extends a hand to contestants facing hate.

	“We all trauma bond together,” Carmona says. “No one understands the experience of what we went through.”

schema.headline: The Rise of ‘Love Island USA’: From Death Threats Against Contestants to Agency Battles for the Biggest Stars

									Getty / Hulu
	

		
	
				
	“Love Overboard” is lost at sea.

	The dating show executive produced by Alex Cooper has been canceled by Hulu, Variety has confirmed.

	Hosted by “The Bachelorette” and “The Traitors” alum Gabby Windey, the reality series followed 22 contestants aboard a luxury yacht who were looking for love while also competing in challenges to gain access to the boat’s amenities.


	The show premiered on March 26 and marked Cooper’s first foray into unscripted television. While “Love Overboard” failed to sail, the “Call Her Daddy” host and her recently launched Unwell Productions banner have a handful of TV projects in the works.
	

	Her dating game show with Harry Jowsey, “Let’s Marry Harry,” debuted on Netflix earlier this month. She launched “Unwell Winter Games” on YouTube earlier this year and will debut a “Summer Games” in early September. Cooper also has a scripted series titled “You Deserve to Know” in development at Hulu starring “Vampire Diaries” favorites Nina Dobrev and Paul Wesley.

	Earlier this year, Cooper executive produced and interviewed Miley Cyrus on Disney+’s “Hannah Montana” 20th anniversary special.

	Page Six was first to report the cancellation of “Love Overboard.”


	
		More from Variety

title: ‘Guardians of the Video Game’ Lands Finecut for International Sales Ahead of Toronto Market
description: Seoul-based sales agent Finecut has acquired international sales rights to “Guardians of the Video Game,” a 3D animated feature based on the Naver W
body:
Seoul-based sales agent Finecut has acquired international sales rights to “Guardians of the Video Game,” a 3D animated feature based on the Naver Webtoon of the same name, ahead of the Toronto market.

	“Guardians of the Video Game” originated as a Naver Webtoon by Gasfard that has amassed 345 million views. The property was later turned into a mobile game on Google Play before reaching the screen as a full 3D animated feature.


	The film imagines a colorful, family-friendly realm concealed just under the surface of video games themselves, populated by a covert guild of guardians tasked with keeping each title operating and preserving every player’s journey. Its central figure, a guardian banished from sleek 3D gaming worlds, tumbles into an obscure, pixel-based RPG. There, working in secret, he steers an unsuspecting hero toward the game’s conclusion while working to expose a plot targeting both him and the game itself.
	

	Uhm Young-sik directs the feature, adding to a filmography that includes the animated film “Running Man: Revengers” and the animation portion of “Yumi’s Cells” Season 1. He earlier co-directed “Red Shoes and the Seven Dwarfs,” a title that reached distribution in 120 countries.

	Animation and VFX studio Locus Animation produces “Guardians of the Video Game.” The company’s credits include “Red Shoes and the Seven Dwarfs” and “Exorcism Chronicles: The Beginning,” the latter of which now has a sequel in production. Locus Animation has built a broader slate around adaptations of popular webtoons, among them “Barkhan” and “Denma.”

	“Guardians of the Video Game” is currently in post-production and slated for release in the fourth quarter of 2026. Its first footage will be revealed through Finecut during the Toronto market. 
	

	Finecut brings several other titles to Toronto this year. “Long Long Night,” a 3D animated feature, will hold its Toronto premiere in the festival’s Centrepiece section. “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” from director Hong Sangsoo, picked up two Pardo Awards at Locarno this year – one for best direction, another for best performance – along with the festival’s Ecumenical Jury Prize.

	Also on the slate is “Dora,” directed by July Jung and starring Kim Do-yeon and Ando Sakura, an invitee to Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight. Park Hoon-jung’s noir “Tristes Tropiques” rounds out the lineup; the film won the Silver Raven Award from Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival and picked up invitations from Sitges, Fantasia, Fantasy Filmfest and L’Étrange Festival.

title: Xolo Maridueña Was Not Sure Blue Beetle Would Ever Come Back, Until James Gunn Called Him About the ‘Superman’ Sequel: ‘The Most Humbled’
description: Xolo Maridueña wasn’t sure what would become of Blue Beetle after he debuted as the DC crime fighter in a 2023 blockbuster. That was, until DC boss
body:
Xolo Maridueña wasn’t sure what would become of Blue Beetle after he debuted as the DC crime fighter in a 2023 blockbuster. That was, until DC boss James Gunn called him about coming back for the “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”

	“I was in Japan with my friends; nobody knew anything,” Maridueña recalled on the red carpet at the Los Angeles premiere of “Practical Magic 2. “And I just see, like the Bat-phone, my phone rings [and it’s] James Gunn. All my friends look at me, and I had to leave the room. I came back, and I was like, ‘Off the record, don’t tell anyone, but we’re coming back,’ and I’m so excited for people to see where Blue Beetle ends up.”
	


	Maridueña explained that he was unsure he’d suit up as Blue Beetle again after his standalone feature. He added that he feels “humbled” by the opportunity to come back to the DCU.


	“There’s never a guarantee with anything, bro,” he said. “I mean, you know this, stuff flips on a dime, and I know that it’s not always like a merit-based system. So there’s so much that’s out of my control, but I am just the most humbled of James and the greater DC team for folding us in, Indiana Jones style.”

	“Man of Tomorrow,” the follow-up to 2025’s “Superman,” sees the titular DC icon team up with his arch-nemesis Lex Luthor to defeat an intergalactic super genius known as Brainiac. David Corenswet and Nicholas Hoult are set to return as Superman and Lex, respectively. Other cast members include Lars Eidinger, Aaron Pierre, Nathan Fillion, Milly Alcock, Isabela Merced and Skyler Gisondo.
	

	Earlier in the interview, Maridueña said it was “surreal” to act alongside Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman for “Practical Magic 2.” He shared that after his first day on set, he was so excited that he wrote down every detail he could remember in his journal.

	“The first day on set with the two of them, you’re having this third-person moment where they’re not only actors that you’ve witnessed your whole life, but also characters that are so electric,” Maridueña explained. “To be in the middle of this Venn diagram, my journal was full that night of all of the stuff, all of the little gems, all of the happy accidents, all of the morsels of knowledge that they give. They are outstanding class acts.”

	“Practical Magic 2,” which hits theaters on Sept. 11, follows Sally, Gillian and their family of witches as they try to break a generational curse that stops them from falling in love. Other cast members include Stockard Channing, Dianne Wiest, Cassie Bradley, Joey King, Maisie Williams and Lee Pace. Susanne Bier directs, with a script by Akiva Goldsman, Georgia Pritchett and Kelly Marcel.

schema.headline: Xolo Maridueña Was Not Sure Blue Beetle Would Ever Come Back, Until James Gunn Called Him About the ‘Superman’ Sequel: ‘The Most Humbled’

title: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis Found Guilty of Orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s Murder
description:
A jury has found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur.

	After a day of closing arguments, Davis was found
body:
A jury has found Duane “Keffe D” Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur.

	After a day of closing arguments, Davis was found guilty of murder with the use of a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang, according to ABC News. Davis, 63, faces a maximum of life in prison.

	The jury deliberated for roughly three hours after a weeks-long trial in Las Vegas. Prosecutors and police claimed that Davis orchestrated Shakur’s murder in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on September 7, 1996, and handed the gunman the murder weapon. They believe that the actual shooter was either Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’ nephew, or another man who was in the backseat of a car.
	

	During his closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal said that the case was “drenched in circumstantial evidence” and corroborating witnesses, in addition to Davis’ own statements over the years to media and in his own memoir to show that he was guilty of aiding the murder. “For nearly 18 years, Duane Davis has told the police, television, books, YouTube interviewers — anybody that will listen, he has told — he is responsible for the murder of Tupac Shakur,” said Palal. “Tell him you hear him — find him guilty.”

	Davis’ attorney Michael Sanft, meanwhile, argued that the only proof that Davis was responsible for Shakur’s murder was through his own confessions, which did not constitute real evidence.

	“We have to ask ourselves the question really at this particular point: Why are we here 30 years later if Duane Davis had actually confessed — truly confessed?” he said.
	

	Davis is scheduled to be sentenced on October 13 and will be held without bail. He shared that he plans to appeal the sentence once it’s handed down.

	On the night of Sept. 7, 1996, Shakur was shot four times with a Glock .22 pistol while his car was stopped at a red light in Paradise, Nev. The bullets came from a white Cadillac that had pulled up alongside Shakur’s vehicle — which was being driven by his label boss, Marion “Suge” Knight — and struck the hip-hop artist in the chest, arm and thigh, while one of the bullets grazed Knight in the head. Shakur succumbed to his injuries six days later.

	Shakur’s murder has long been one of music’s most notorious unsolved crimes. Over the years, Davis boasted about his purported role in Shakur’s killing. In 2018, to drum up anticipation for his upcoming memoir, he appeared in the BET docuseries “Death Row Chronicles,” where he discussed the night of Shakur’s murder, suggesting that the murder weapon was passed from someone in the backseat of the white Cadillac, but he wouldn’t say who. “Going to keep it for the code of the streets,” Davis remarked, adding, “It just came from the backseat, bro.”

	Davis released his memoir, “Compton Street Legend,” in 2019, whose intro stated, “I’m one of the only living eyewitnesses to Tupac’s killing,” before describing the night of Shakur’s killing in detail. In the book, Davis claims that he got a Glock and entered the white Cadillac with three others, looking for payback against Shakur and Knight for what they’d done to Anderson. “No words exchanged, the time for talking had passed, the shit was about to go down!” he wrote.

	Prosecutors brought the case against Davis in September 2023, claiming he orchestrated the murder after Shakur’s entourage attacked his nephew just hours before Shakur’s death at age 25.

schema.headline: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis Found Guilty of Orchestrating Tupac Shakur’s Murder

title: SND Swoops on Toronto-Bound Bérénice Bejo Starrer  ‘Alice: Pioneer of Cinema’ Ahead of Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Paris-based film and television studio SND, part of French media group M6, has picked up world sales on the high-end period drama “Alice: Pioneer of
body:
Paris-based film and television studio SND, part of French media group M6, has picked up world sales on the high-end period drama “Alice: Pioneer of Cinema,” in which Oscar-nominee Bérénice Bejo (“The Artist”) stars as Alice Guy, the very first female fiction filmmaker.The six-parter, ordered by HBO Max and France Télévisions, is due to world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival‘s Primetime section on Sept. 14, ahead of its airing in December.

	France’s Wild Bunch and Ligne de Front are producing along with Belgium’s Panache Productions, La Compagnie Cinématographique and Canada’s Sphere Media.The big-scale series, created by Tim Loane (“Versailles,” “Das Boot”) and Claire Lemaréchal (“The Bureau”) from a script by André Gulluni (“Rematch”), will also play on the leading Spanish pay TV/SVOD service Movistar Plus+, HBO Max in Belgium and the streamer Crave in Canada.



	

					‘Alice: Pioneer of Cinema’
									Credit: Caroline Dubois/SND/Wild Bunch/France Télévisions
	



	Helmed by Virginie Verrier and Guillaume Lonergan, “Alice: Pioneer of Cinema” tells the true story of Alice Guy, who turned from secretary for Gaumont to the first female fiction filmmaker and movie mogul in the late 19th to early 20th century. 

	After rising through the ranks at French banner Gaumont, she moves to the U.S., where she builds the first film studio owned by a woman. Despite her extraordinary achievements, she ends up losing it all, and her name fades into oblivion.

	A century later, her film pioneering role is finally recognized when she receives a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award from the Directors Guild of America, handed out by Martin Scorsese. Then in 2024, at the Paris Olympic Games, her golden statue rises from the Seine, alongside other female luminaries Simon Veil and Simone de Beauvoir. 

	Besides Bejo, the stellar cast takes in Oscar Lesage (“The Substance”), Thibaut Evrard (“Paris Police 1900,” “No Man’s Land”), Irène Jacob (“The Affair; “The Double Life of Véronique”), Sophie Nélisse (“Yellowjackets,” “The Book Thief”) and François Arnaud (“The Borgias,” “Yellowjackets”).

	“Every so often, a series arrives with a story so extraordinary you cannot believe it has never been told,” said Alexis Reybet-Degat, SND head of international TV series distribution. “‘Alice’ has the scale and craft of a major production, and a heroine whose fight feels strikingly modern. It is prestige and popular at once, and we are proud to bring it to broadcasters around the world.”
	

	Caroline De Jenlis, producer at Ligne de Front said, “We are thrilled to partner with SND. With their incredible expertise, we are fully confident they will give Alice’s extraordinary story the global showcase it deserves.”

	SND will start negotiating the series at the 32nd Unifrance Rendez Vous in Le Havre, unspooling over Sept 7-10. Another prime drama on the sales banner’s slate includes the nuclear warship thriller “R91.”

	In Toronto, “Alice: Pioneer of Cinema” will be showcased together with nine premium shows from major players such as A24, Amazon MGM, Netflix and Apple.
